problems.stem: A reviewer says 'this screen looks clean, so it is accessible.' What is the strongest correction?
options: Agree, since clean layouts are usually accessible.
Check the screen against named WCAG criteria such as alt text, contrast, and color-only cues; appearance is not a finding.
Add more whitespace until it looks even cleaner.
Ask a colleague whether they also think it looks clean.
problems.explanation: Accessibility findings come from specific success criteria, not from how polished the screen appears.

problems.stem: The only cue for the required next action is 'the red frame is next.' Which WCAG issue does this raise?
options: It is fine because red is easy to see.
Conveying the action by color alone fails use-of-color (1.4.1); add a text label and an icon.
It only affects the font size.
It is a contrast problem, so just darken the red.
problems.explanation: Color alone excludes color-blind learners; the action must be conveyed in more than one channel.

problems.stem: A reviewer uses AI to draft alt text for a content-bearing diagram. What is the strongest boundary?
options: Accept the AI alt text unread because it is grammatical.
Use the AI draft as a starting point, then check it names what the diagram shows and why it matters before accepting.
Leave the alt text empty since the image is decorative.
Ask AI only to make the alt text longer.
problems.explanation: AI can draft alt text, but the reviewer must verify it conveys the diagram's content and purpose (WCAG 1.1.1).

problems.stem: Three blockers are found: missing alt text, 2.9:1 contrast, and a color-only action cue. Which fix should go first and why?
options: Contrast, because it is the easiest to change.
Alt text, because the missing description fully excludes a screen-reader user from the content.
The color cue, because color is the most noticeable.
Any order, since all three are equally urgent.
problems.explanation: Prioritize by who is fully excluded; a screen-reader user gets nothing from an undescribed content image.
